PURPOSE

This technical description is intended for the study of the KM1801VM2 integrated circuit and serves as a supplement to Part I of the technical description of this integrated circuit.

INTRODUCTION

The KM1801VM2 integrated circuit is a single-chip 16-bit microprocessor of increased functional complexity, intended for processing digital information in general-purpose equipment.

As part of a computer system, the microprocessor can be used for process control, instrumentation and measurement equipment, communication systems, and for solving engineering, technical, and economic problems.

pages.translation:
1. GENERAL PRINCIPLES OF KM1801VM2 MICROPROCESSOR ORGANIZATION

The KM1801VM2 integrated circuit is a single-chip 16-bit microprocessor.
No additional hardware is required for its operation.

The internal microprogram control unit provides execution of the entire
instruction set of the Elektronika-60 computer, except for floating-point
instructions and console-mode instructions.

For complete compatibility with the Elektronika-60 instruction set, the
microprocessor provides the possibility of operating with a system ROM,
in which additional instructions may be implemented.

The system ROM may be organized in such a way that its address space does
not occupy addresses within the main addressing area. This is achieved by
introducing an additional 17th address bit, which allows the processor's
address space to be doubled.

The additional address-space area is used not only for extending the
instruction set, but also for implementing various bootstrap modes.

To accept bootstrap conditions, the microprocessor includes a special
address-less read procedure. During this procedure an external bootstrap
condition register is read, in which the high-order byte of the system
memory address is stored.

Upon initial power-up, the processor reads this register using the
address-less read procedure, forms an address from the information read,
and loads the program counter from that address.

The address is then incremented by 2 and the Processor Status Register
(PSW) is loaded.

After that, if there are no unmasked interrupts, the microprocessor
begins program execution.

The bootstrap condition register is read not only during initial startup,
but also during execution of the HALT instruction and during the handling
of certain fatal conditions.

Further details...

All of these features are described in detail in the corresponding sections below.

The microprocessor implements a pipelined principle of instruction
fetch and execution. The operation of the microprocessor is organized
such that by the end of processing the i-th instruction, the (i+1)-th
instruction has already been fetched into an internal buffer register,
and fetching of the (i+2)-th instruction has begun.

Special cases that disrupt the pipeline are detected by hardware.
All such cases are described in detail in Section 4.

The microprocessor contains an internal interrupt unit. It provides
priority handling of all interrupts, both external and internal.
Interrupt processing and interrupt-vector generation are performed
by the microprocessor without the use of any additional integrated
circuits.

All arithmetic and logical operations on operands, as well as the
calculation of operand and instruction addresses, are performed in
the processor's operational unit. The operational unit processes
both 16-bit words and 8-bit bytes. It also generates the condition
codes resulting from operations and stores them in the Processor
Status Register.

To execute multiplication, division, and arithmetic shift operations,
the microprocessor includes a special extended-arithmetic unit.
The use of this unit significantly reduces execution time for the
extended arithmetic instructions compared with a purely microprogrammed
implementation. The size of the microprogram memory is also
significantly reduced.

To reduce the size of the main microprogram memory, a special branch-
condition processing unit has been incorporated into the microprocessor.
